title: Dependency injection and IoC
idea: Dependency injection (DI) means a class receives the objects it needs instead of creating them; inversion of control (IoC) is the wider idea that outside code drives yours.

analogy.text: A camera body accepts any lens that fits its mount. The photographer chooses and attaches the lens; the camera never builds one.
analogy.breaks: JavaScript does not check the mount; a wrong object fails at call time.

points: A class that calls `new` on its helpers is welded to them.
Constructor injection passes helpers in, so the class depends only on their methods.
One composition root, near `main`, decides which concrete classes to wire together.
IoC means the outside calls and configures you; a DI container automates the wiring.

hero.title: Who creates what, who calls what

edges.label: creates
edges.caption: Only the composition root uses `new` on concrete helpers.

edges.label: injects mailer
edges.caption: It hands the mailer to `SignupService` through the constructor.

edges.label: calls
edges.caption: `SignupService` knows only that the object has `send(to, text)`.

edges.label: fits
edges.caption: A test injects `FakeMailer` instead. `SignupService` does not change.

code.title: Constructor injection
code.caption: One service, two mailers. Write a `LoudMailer` that upper-cases the text and inject it.

walk.text: A fake that records calls, so a test can check them.
The service stores what it is given; it never calls `new` on a mailer.
It relies only on `send(to, text)`: dependency inversion in practice.
The composition root picks the concrete class in one place.
Swap in the fake and inspect what would have been sent.

code.title: A tiny DI container
code.caption: A container maps names to factories and builds each object once. Frameworks add scopes and auto-wiring on top.

walk.text: Two maps: how to build each thing, and what is already built.
Return the cached instance, so every caller shares one object.
Fail loudly when nothing was registered under that name.
The factory receives the container, so it can resolve its own dependencies.
`greeter` asks for `config`; it never knows how `config` is built.

pitfalls: Do not pass the container into business classes; that hides dependencies again.
A constructor with a long list of dependencies signals a class doing too much.
Avoid default `new Helper()` parameters in core logic; they quietly re-weld the dependency.

quiz.why: The default builds a `Repo` only when nothing is passed, which quietly re-welds it. The second call injects the fake, so its `find` runs.

takeaway: Classes ask for their helpers; one composition root decides which ones.
